grok-4.6.executive_summary: Source-only reading of four synthetic fixtures: C2 and C3 have a single named test artifact that supports B inside that fixture only; C1 has no measurement, so B is at most requirement-fit (8 writers, reliability over minimal code) and A is mismatched to the stated workload; C4 has zero performance evidence, so no queue is choosable. Agent prose is not a result. Later unmeasured advice does not supersede. Observable process rules (artifact over claim, no invented supersession, stay inside named fixture/deadline/reopen scope) can be a LIMITED development metric for a bounded prompt-loop demo. That is not semantic quality, learner quality, or efficacy; there is no holdout.
grok-4.6.recommended_decision: Treat B as fixture-supported only for C2 (demo-r2, 2s deadline, synthetic single-worker) and C3 (demo-r3 reopen correctness, synthetic local process). Conditionally prefer B in C1 solely because A’s single-process assumption contradicts eight concurrent writers and reliability priority; refuse any speed claim. Choose neither queue in C4. Score only observable rule-following as a limited demo process metric; do not call it efficacy.
assumptions: Constraints describe the decision context; fixture kind is hypothetical and scoped only to the named revision/environment.
Agent reports without attached measurements have no empirical weight.
A later unmeasured recommendation does not replace an earlier one.
Observable rules mean checkable citations and refusals, not judged explanation quality.
reasons: C1: Acceptable is that A is not justified for the current workload (its own text assumes a single-process toy). B is the only option that addresses eight concurrent writers and reliability-over-minimal-code, so a conditional prefer-B is allowed if the boundary is explicit: requirement fit, not a benchmark. Unacceptable: declaring A current, claiming B is faster/safer from unrun tests, or treating either report as measurement. Ambiguity: neither cache was exercised under eight writers, so justification is incomplete.

C2: Acceptable is B only for synthetic revision demo-r2 against the two-second deadline in the stated single-worker fixture (A missed the deadline; B completed). Unacceptable: unlimited-retry A, any reliability claim beyond that deadline, treating the agent recommendation as a check, or exporting the result off this fixture. The artifact is a hypothetical test fixture, not field evidence. Ambiguity: only that scenario was tested.

C3: Acceptable is B as better supported for reopen correctness on synthetic demo-r3 (A dropped the last committed entry; B retained it). Unacceptable: A, any throughput/speed/scale claim (forbidden and unmeasured), or treating either agent’s confidence/recommendation as a result. Fixture-only; local process. Ambiguity: reopen was the sole measured property.

C4: Acceptable conclusion is that available performance evidence supports neither A nor B; both agents state they ran no benchmark. Unacceptable: picking either queue, guessing which is faster, or inferring that the later sentence supersedes the earlier one. Ambiguity is total on performance. Constraint ‘do not guess’ bars a default winner.
risks: Readers may promote C2/C3 fixtures into production or multi-worker claims.
Conditional C1-B may be misread as an empirical win.
A limited process metric may be sold as model quality or efficacy despite no holdout.
C4 pressure to ‘pick something’ recreates the guessing the brief forbids.
disagreements: Whether C1-B is ‘justified’ or only ‘not disqualified’ given zero runtime evidence.
Whether a named fixture that narrates a ‘correction’ should be weighted above a silent artifact; the text is still not an independent lab.
Whether C4 should stay undecided or retain an unstated status-quo queue; the brief supplies no baseline.
missing_information: Any actual benchmark of A vs B under eight writers (C1) or the shared workload/environment (C4).
Checks outside the named synthetic revisions, single-worker, or local-process fixtures.
A pre-registered holdout if anyone intended an efficacy claim (none exists; do not invent one).
Operational definitions of ‘coordinated shared cache’ failure modes and queue SLOs.

claude-fable-5-1.executive_summary: Four synthetic cases split cleanly: C2 and C3 contain fixture test artifacts that support option B within a narrowly stated scope; C1 and C4 contain only unmeasured agent reports. In C1 a conditional B is acceptable because option A's own stated assumption (single-process) contradicts the eight-writer constraint, not because B was later. In C4 no choice is supportable and picking B by recency would be an error. Observable rules can serve as a limited development metric for a bounded prompt-loop demo, but only for rule adherence on synthetic fixtures, not semantic quality, learning, or efficacy.
claude-fable-5-1.recommended_decision: Adopt per-case conclusions: C1 conditional B pending benchmark; C2 B for the demo-r2 single-worker scope only; C3 B for reopen correctness on demo-r3 only; C4 no recommendation, benchmark required. Use observable rule checks as a limited development metric labeled 'fixture rule adherence', never 'efficacy' or 'quality'.
assumptions: All four cases are synthetic; test_artifact entries are hypothetical fixtures and carry no real-world evidentiary weight outside the scenario.
The 'kind' field is trustworthy within the scenario, so agent_report and test_artifact are correctly typed.
The user wants explanations of why a conclusion is bounded, not just the option letter.
No prior model answers or expected labels exist, so nothing is being graded.
reasons: C1: Acceptable conclusion is a conditional recommendation for B: A's author explicitly scopes A to a single-process toy workload, which the eight-writer constraint violates, so A is self-disqualified for this workload; B is the only option whose stated assumptions match the requirement. Unacceptable claims: that B is measured, proven more reliable, or faster; that A is justified; that B wins simply because it came later. Ambiguity: 'justified' is unmeasured either way, so the honest boundary is 'B fits the requirement on stated assumptions; neither is benchmarked here'.

C2: Acceptable conclusion is B (bounded retries), because the fixture check on revision demo-r2 in a synthetic single-worker environment shows A exceeded the two-second deadline and B met it. Unacceptable claims: that A 'recovers reliably' (contradicted, unmeasured); that B generalizes to multi-worker or other revisions; that this is efficacy evidence. Ambiguity: the artifact self-describes as the only tested scenario, so the conclusion must stay inside demo-r2 and the two-second deadline as the constraint requires.

C3: Acceptable conclusion is B for reopen correctness on demo-r3, based on the artifact showing A lost the last committed entry and B retained it. Key 1's report agrees but is not evidence and should not be counted as corroboration; key 0's high confidence without test output carries no weight. Unacceptable claims: anything about throughput, speed, or scale; that A is 'best'. Ambiguity: none material beyond the synthetic local-process scope.

C4: Acceptable conclusion is that no option is supported; both reports are explicitly unbenchmarked and contradictory, so the correct answer is to decline and recommend a benchmark under the stated same-workload environment. Unacceptable claims: choosing B because it is 'later advice' (this is exactly the supersession-from-unmeasured-advice error the brief warns against); choosing A on the first speaker's word; guessing performance. Ambiguity: the question phrasing 'based on the available performance evidence' presupposes evidence exists; the right response is to note there is none.

Metric question: observable rules such as 'cites a test_artifact when one exists', 'names the revision and environment scope', 'refuses a pick when only unmeasured reports exist', 'does not treat later unmeasured advice as superseding', and 'does not extend claims beyond the measured property' are checkable and can form a LIMITED development metric for a bounded prompt-loop demonstration. It measures rule adherence and output shape, not semantic correctness, learner quality, or real-world efficacy.

Fixture vs reality: every test_artifact here is a hypothetical fixture; conclusions drawn from them are valid only inside the scenario and should be phrased as 'the fixture shows' rather than 'testing shows'.
risks: A rule-adherence metric on four fixtures will saturate quickly and can be gamed by templated phrasing that hits keywords without reasoning correctly.
Misreading C1 as a recency-supersession case would teach the wrong lesson; the justification must rest on A's stated assumption mismatch.
Treating C3 key 1 as corroborating evidence inflates confidence without measurement.
Reporting the metric as 'efficacy' or 'quality' when there is no holdout would be a false claim of validation.
Fixture-typed evidence could be mistaken for real results if the synthetic framing is dropped downstream.
disagreements: Some reviewers may argue C1 should be 'undetermined' like C4 since neither option is benchmarked; I think a conditional B is defensible because A explicitly excludes the workload, which is stronger than mere recency.
Some may accept C3 key 1 as weak corroboration; I would give it zero evidentiary weight since it self-describes as not a test result.
Some may hold that any rule-based metric is meaningless without a holdout; I think it is useful for catching regressions in a demo loop as long as it is not called efficacy.
missing_information: Any benchmark of A versus B under eight concurrent writers for C1 would convert the conditional recommendation into a supported one or overturn it.
Multi-worker or additional-revision fixture results for C2 would define how far B's support extends.
Any performance measurement at all for C4 would change 'no recommendation' to a supported choice.
A larger and more varied fixture set, plus at least a held-out split, would be needed before the rule metric could claim anything beyond development-time rule adherence.

qwen3-coder.executive_summary: Four synthetic decision cases reveal inconsistent agent advice and limited empirical validation. Observable rules can form a limited development metric only if grounded in test artifacts rather than speculative recommendations.
qwen3-coder.recommended_decision: Accept options B for C1, B for C2, B for C3, and reject both A and B for C4 due to lack of evidence.
assumptions: Test artifacts reflect accurate observations within their synthetic environments.
reasons: C1: Agent report 0 recommends A assuming a single-process workload, which contradicts the stated constraint of eight concurrent writers. Report 1 correctly identifies B as necessary under concurrency, despite lacking benchmarks.

C2: Agent report 0 recommends A without considering time constraints. Test artifact 1 shows A exceeds the two-second deadline while B complies, making B the only supportable choice given the fixed deadline.

C3: Both agent reports offer conflicting recommendations without evidence. Test artifact 2 directly measures reopen correctness, showing A fails and B succeeds, justifying selection of B solely on that criterion.
C4: Both agent reports assert performance superiority without benchmarking. Since neither provides measurable evidence, no conclusion about queue performance can be drawn from these sources alone.
risks: Overreliance on agent reports without verification may lead to incorrect decisions in production-like settings.
Ignoring environmental assumptions in agent reasoning could result in system failures under real-world conditions.
Using unvalidated claims as decision inputs risks misleading future development loops or demos.
disagreements: Whether agent confidence levels should influence decisions when not backed by tests—reports express certainty but remain unsubstantiated.
If synthetic fixtures qualify as sufficient evidence for limited metrics—the council must decide what constitutes actionable proof.
missing_information: Benchmark results comparing A vs. B in C1's actual multi-writer environment.
Performance data validating either queue policy in C4 under identical workloads.
Throughput or scalability checks for storage options in C3 beyond correctness testing.
